2	
3	Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>

10	## Current sprint: Sprint 3
11	
12	- **Dates:** Nov 3 – Nov 19, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Nov 19, 11:59 PM**, except
13	  the D7 check-in, due **Nov 12, 11:59 PM** together with at least one code PR of your own, open
14	  and ready for review or merged.
15	- **Focus:** testing, meaning how well the tests check what the code is supposed to do.
16	- **Points:** 100.
17	- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D8) or no release (D9) means **0 for the
18	  whole sprint**.
19	- **Carries forward:** anything the Sprint 3 page doesn't change comes from the Sprint 2 and
20	  Sprint 1 pages, and every Sprint 0 standard still applies.

37	### Graded strictly this sprint
38	
39	The Sprint 3 page lists these as the rules that cost the most points. Details are in the sections
40	named.
41	
42	1. No merge without a teammate's approval on the PR's **latest commit** (Reviews, below).
43	2. A spec review comment on the issue that says what was checked (Spec review, under the issue
44	   formats).
45	3. Every code PR has `Closes #<N>`, and both the issue and the PR are on the `Sprint 3` milestone.
46	4. Real AI logs, linked from the issue (D5).
47	5. A Test Evidence table in every PR, with expected values not copied from the code's output
48	   (Pull request format).
49	6. Mutation testing with a tool, with before and after reports committed (Mutation testing (D6)).
50	7. The team introduces no new test failures. A skipped test or a disabled CI check needs a linked
51	   issue and a reason in a code comment (D8).
52	8. A sprint report that renders on GitHub and uses the Sprint 3 sections (D8).
53	
54	### Deliverable notes
55	
56	- **D1 load:** each CSCI 435 student owns at least 2 medium issues; each CSCI 535 student owns at
57	  least 2 medium and 1 small. Either load can be met with equivalent story points instead. Every
58	  issue has exactly **one** assignee. Unfinished Sprint 2 issues go into the backlog before new
59	  work. To drop one, write the reason on that issue. If the backlog is too thin to meet the load,
60	  find areas that still need work (features, improvements, test gaps, bugs) and write new issues
61	  for them the usual way.
62	- **D1 scope:** every issue states its scope (small or medium) and one or two sentences on why:
63	  which components it touches and how much change is expected. The instructor or TA may reclassify
64	  an issue whose scope is clearly overstated.
65	- **D1 hardening issues (optional):** one of your issues may be a hardening issue. See "Hardening
66	  issues" below.
67	- **D1 team feature:** the instructor or TA posts a larger feature for Sprints 3–4 as an issue and
68	  tells the team. Split it into sub-issues, each with one owner, its own spec (D2) and scope, linked
69	  to the feature issue and added to the `Sprint 3` milestone. Sub-issues count toward the load.
70	- **D2:** specs are written and spec-reviewed before coding starts. Features use the user story
71	  format; hardening issues use the bug report format when they fix a defect, otherwise the
72	  hardening task format.
73	- **D3:** each decision names at least two concrete alternatives and why one won; this is graded
74	  strictly. The site also accepts the decision in an issue comment or the PR description; the team
75	  keeps it in the issue body. Decisions that span issues go in `docs/sprint3/design.md`.
76	- **D4:** every PR description has the Test Evidence and Tech Debt sections (see "Pull request
77	  format"). Per-PR scores are combined across your PRs and scaled to 20.
78	- **D5:** conventions are in `ai-logs/README.md`. Logs hold the full prompts and output. Graded
79	  strictly this sprint: a session summary, paraphrased prompts, a share link, or tool output without
80	  the prompts that produced it is not a log. The link must open the log file itself, not a folder
81	  or another issue. The folder must exist even if no AI was used; in that case, post a comment
82	  saying so. The site accepts the link from the issue or the PR; the team keeps it in **issue
83	  comments only** (`AI-ASSISTANCE.md`).
84	- **D6:** see "Mutation testing (D6)" below.
85	- **D7:** about 100 words on each of: what you have implemented so far and what remains; one thing
86	  you learned about testing in the project; one risk to finishing by Nov 19 and what you will do
87	  about it. Link at least one **code PR you authored**, open and ready for review or merged, by Nov
88	  12. On time, substantive and with a PR linked scores 5; late, thin or no PR 3; missing 0.
89	- **D8:** graded on completeness, specificity, quality of evidence and the Suite health section;
90	  sections are in "Sprint report (D8) sections" below.
91	- **D9:** keep the base version (`v1.27.3-csci435-s2` → `v1.27.3-csci435-s3`). Tag **after the
92	  last Sprint 3 merge**, so the release matches the final `main`, and push the tag to origin. The
93	  release description summarizes the sprint's features, fixes and hardening work, not just the tag
94	  name.
95	- **Reviews:** nobody approves or merges their own PR. Request the review on GitHub and tell the
96	  reviewer on Zulip; reviewers respond (approve or request changes) within 24 hours, with
97	  substantive comments and the rubric, not a bare approval. A PR is merged only after a teammate
98	  approves its **latest commit**: any push after the approval, including merging `main` in, needs
99	  a new approval. Once approved, the author merges. Each student reviews at least one PR per
100	  sprint, and every teammate at least once per semester.
101	- **Extra credit:** up to 3 points per PR submitted to upstream Gitea that is accepted or under
102	  active review, and up to 2 points per bug report filed upstream that comes from your own testing
103	  and is confirmed by the maintainers by the time Sprint 4 is graded. Both at the instructor's
104	  discretion.

106	## Branches and commits
107	
108	- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
109	  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
110	- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
111	  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
112	  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
113	  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

115	### Before each implementation: sync with main
116	
117	Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:
118	
119	```bash
120	git switch main
121	git pull origin main
122	git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
123	```
124	
125	To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
126	or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):
127	
128	```bash
129	git fetch origin
130	git merge origin/main
131	```
132	
133	Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. A merge pushed after
134	approval needs a new approval (see Reviews). Never merge another feature branch into yours.
135	
136	### After merge: clean up
137	
138	A PR is merged with a merge commit once its latest commit is approved, every review comment is
139	addressed and CI passes. Then:
140	
141	```bash
142	git switch main
143	git pull origin main
144	git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
145	git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
146	git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
147	```
148	
149	Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), that the issue and PR are on the sprint
150	milestone, and that the issue has its AI Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the
151	session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).
152	
153	## Issue format: feature (user story)
154	
155	Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
156	Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
157	
158	```markdown
159	## User Story
160	As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.
161	
162	## User Scenario
163	<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>
164	
165	## Acceptance Criteria
166	- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
167	- [ ] AC2: ...
168	- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)
169	
170	## Out of Scope
171	- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>
172	
173	## Open Questions
174	- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>
175	
176	## Design Decision
177	**Decision:** <what was chosen>
178	**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
179	**Rationale:** <why this one>
180	**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>
181	
182	## Scope
183	small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
184	<One or two sentences on why: the components it touches and how much change you expect.>
185	```
186	
187	## Issue format: bug report
188	
189	Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`. Also used by hardening issues that fix a
190	defect.
191	
192	```markdown
193	## Observed Behavior
194	## Expected Behavior
195	## Steps to Reproduce
196	1. ...
197	## Additional Information
198	<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
199	## Design Decision
200	<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
201	## Scope
202	<Same as above: size, label and one or two sentences on why.>
203	```
204	
205	## Issue format: hardening task
206	
207	No GitHub template; write it in a blank issue. Used by hardening issues that don't fix a defect,
208	such as a flaky test or a broken CI check (Sprint 3, D2).
209	
210	```markdown
211	## Problem
212	<What is unreliable now, and how you know: failing test names, run counts, CI run links.>
213	## Goal
214	<What "fixed" means.>
215	## Acceptance Criteria
216	- [ ] AC1: ...
217	## Evidence of Fix
218	<Which evidence from the table below the fix will show.>
219	## Design Decision
220	<Same four fields as above.>
221	## Scope
222	<Same as above: size, label and one or two sentences on why.>
223	```
224	
225	### Hardening issues
226	
227	Work that makes the existing system more reliable rather than adding a feature. Good sources: the
228	D8 baseline run (failing or flaky tests, broken CI checks on `main`); the "Introduced" and
229	"Encountered" Tech Debt fields of Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 PRs; bugs found in reviews or after
230	merging; and the upstream issue tracker for the parts of Gitea the team works on. It is scoped like
231	any other issue and must include evidence that the problem is fixed:
232	
233	| Kind | Evidence |
234	| --- | --- |
235	| Bug fix | A test that fails before the fix and passes after |
236	| Flaky test | The root cause, and repeated runs before and after the fix (e.g. 20 for a unit test, 10 for E2E) |
237	| Broken or missing CI check | Links to CI runs before and after the fix |
238	| Failing tests in the baseline | Pass/fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group of failures |
239	
240	The site doesn't say where the evidence goes: plan it in the issue (Evidence of Fix, or Additional
241	Information for a bug), then post the results on the issue and in the PR's Test Evidence once the
242	fix is in. Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause
243	counts as small at most.
244	
245	### Design Decision and spec review
246	
247	- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
248	  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
249	  the issue body.
250	- **Spec review (D2):** before coding starts, a teammate posts a review comment **on the issue**.
251	  Start it with `Spec reviewed` so it is easy to find. The layout is the reviewer's choice, but the
252	  comment must say what was checked:
253	  1. each acceptance criterion: clear and testable, naming any that aren't;
254	  2. the cases considered (e.g. empty input, errors, permissions) and whether the ACs cover them;
255	  3. whether the scope fits the stated size;
256	
257	  and end with an approval, or the problems for the author to fix in the spec. `Looks good!` with
258	  nothing about what was checked does not count. An optional layout:
259	
260	  ```markdown
261	  Spec reviewed — @reviewer-username
262	
263	  **Acceptance criteria:** <clear and testable? which aren't, and why>
264	  **Cases considered:** <which cases, and whether the ACs cover them>
265	  **Scope:** <does it fit the stated size?>
266	  **Verdict:** Approved | Changes needed: <list>
267	  ```
268	
269	## Pull request format
270	
271	Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
272	`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:
273	
274	1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge. Every code PR links its issue, and
275	   the PR goes on the `Sprint 3` milestone too.
276	2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
277	3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
278	4. **Test Evidence:** required from Sprint 3. It replaces the old "How it was tested" section.
279	   Every behaviour change still needs a new or updated test.
280	
281	   ```markdown
282	   ## Test Evidence
283	
284	   | Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
285	   |---|---|---|---|
286	   | AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |
287	
288	   **Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]
289	
290	   **AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]
291	   ```
292	
293	   - **One row per acceptance criterion** from the issue; for a bug report, the Expected Behavior.
294	     A PR that changes no product behaviour (e.g. a CI change) writes `N/A` and why.
295	   - **Test(s):** the test name, plus the file if not obvious. For a manual check, write `Manual:`
296	     followed by the steps and what you saw. An AC tested both ways lists both in the same row.
297	   - **Level:** `unit`, `integration`, `E2E` or `manual`.
298	   - **Source of expected value:** `AC`, `issue discussion`, `docs`, `upstream behavior`, or
299	     `other` (explain). **Never the current output of your own code:** a test whose expected value
300	     was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
301	   - **Not tested automatically, and why:** only for ACs checked manually only.
302	   - AI may draft this section; the author checks that it is accurate.
303	
304	5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status. If CI doesn't run your tests, the commands you ran and
305	   a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).
306	6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
307	7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:
308	
309	   ```markdown
310	   ## Tech Debt
311	
312	   **Introduced:** <shortcuts, workarounds or design compromises this PR makes, and why>
313	
314	   **Encountered:** <tech debt that was already there and that you ran into, and how you handled it>
315	   ```
316	
317	8. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.
318	
319	Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6; tests written or updated
320	appropriately, with the Test Evidence section complete, every AC covered and expected values
321	justified 6; description explains what and why, Tech Debt section present, issue linked 3; CI passes
322	or manual verification documented 3; reviewed with the rubric (including the test evidence row),
323	reviewer comment posted, merged only after an approval on the latest commit 2.
324	
325	## Code review rubric
326	
327	The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
328	is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
329	can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
330	(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
331	below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.
332	
333	```markdown
334	### Code Review — @reviewer-username
335	
336	**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>
337	
338	| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
339	| --- | --- | --- |
340	| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
341	| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
342	| Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally? | | |
343	| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
344	| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
345	| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
346	| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
347	```
348	
349	## Mutation testing (D6)
350	
351	A mutation testing tool makes small changes to the code (*mutants*), such as flipping a condition
352	or a boundary value, and runs the tests against each one. If a test fails, the mutant is
353	**killed**. If every test passes, it **survived**: the tests didn't notice the change, which points
354	to a weak or missing test. An **equivalent** mutant behaves exactly like the original code, so no
355	test can kill it. Definitions are in the course Glossary.
356	
357	**Which issue:** one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests (CSCI 535: two, and the
358	small issue may be one of them). A tool is required; mutating code by hand doesn't count.
359	
360	| Code changed | Tool |
361	| --- | --- |
362	| Frontend TypeScript (Vitest) | StrykerJS with the Vitest runner |
363	| Go backend | Gremlins or go-mutesting |
364	
365	1. Run the tool on the **source files changed by your PR(s)** for that issue, not the whole
366	   project.
367	2. Analyse every surviving mutant: equivalent, or a gap in your tests? If more than 10 survive,
368	   analyse at least 10, starting with lines your PR added or changed.
369	3. Add or strengthen **at least one test that kills a survivor** that revealed a gap, and re-run
370	   the tool to confirm it is killed. If no survivor reveals a gap (all killed or equivalent), say so
371	   and justify it in the surviving-mutants table; that completes this step.
372	4. Answer the three questions in the write-up.
373	
374	Files:
375	
376	- Write-up: `docs/sprint3/mutation/<issue#>-<github-username>.md`, using the template below.
377	- Reports: machine-readable output of the first run and the re-run, as
378	  `docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue#>-<github-username>-before.json` and `-after.json` (`.txt`
379	  for go-mutesting). StrykerJS: add `"json"` to `reporters`. Gremlins: `--output=<file>.json`.
380	  go-mutesting: save the terminal output to a text file. The scores in the write-up must match the
381	  reports, and the mutant your new test kills must show as killed in the "after" report.
382	- The tool configuration you used, committed and linked from the write-up. Reusing a teammate's
383	  setup is encouraged, as long as you run the tool yourself and credit them. The team's shared
384	  setup (go-mutesting for Go), its commands and its pitfalls: `.claude-students/docs/mutation-testing.md`.
385	
386	Common problems:
387	
388	- **The tool stops before mutating.** It first runs the selected tests on unchanged code and stops
389	  if any fail. Fix or exclude them first; the D8 baseline shows which ones fail already.
390	- **Tests run against built code.** Mutants in the source are never seen by tests that run on
391	  compiled output. Configure a rebuild, or pick tests that run on source.
392	- **Tests need services.** Start the database or service first. How each test type runs is in
393	  `.claude-students/docs/testing.md`.
394	- **False survivors.** When limiting which tests run, include the tests that cover the mutated
395	  files. Otherwise mutants they would catch show as survived or not covered. Check that the
396	  relevant tests ran before writing a new test for a survivor.
397	- **Blocked?** Ask teammates first. Then tell the TA **as early as possible**, with the errors and
398	  the AI log of what you tried; the TA may approve a different issue or area. Problems reported at
399	  the end of the sprint don't excuse a missing D6.
400	
401	Template, copied from the Sprint 3 page:
402	
403	```markdown
404	# Mutation testing: Issue #<N> -- <issue title>
405	
406	**PR(s):** #...  **Tool:** ...  **Config:** [link; credit the teammate if you reused their setup]  **Command:** `...`
407	**Reports:** [before](reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json) · [after](reports/<issue#>-<username>-after.json)
408	**Mutation score:** before ...% → after ...%
409	
410	## Surviving mutants
411	
412	| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |
413	|---|---|---|---|
414	| | | | |
415	
416	## New or strengthened test
417	
418	Commit: [link] · Test: [file › test name] · Kills: [mutant location]
419	
420	## Questions
421	
422	1. What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?
423	2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements? Explain.
424	3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct? If AI was not used, write "N/A."
425	```
426	
427	Grading (15 points): tool run on the files changed by the PR, with configuration, command, results
428	and reports committed 4; surviving mutants analysed correctly (equivalent or test gap, with an
429	explanation) 4; at least one new or strengthened test kills a survivor, confirmed by the re-run 4;
430	answers show understanding, not just description 3. CSCI 535: the average of the two write-ups.
431	
432	## Sprint report (D8) sections
433	
434	`docs/sprint<N>/report.md` (or `.pdf` or `.docx`), following `docs/sprint0/report.md`:
435	
436	- Team: names, GitHub usernames, project name, repository link.
437	- Sprint overview.
438	- Backlog: milestone link, why the team chose these issues, plus a table of title, owner, points,
439	  scope and status.
440	- Requirements and design: when specs were done, what surprised you, design rationale.
441	- Completed issues: title, owner, PR link, author, reviewer, what changed.
442	- Test strategy, including untestable changes and why.
443	- AI tool usage per member: tools, session count, AI log folder link, and 2–3 sentences on lessons
444	  learned.
445	- Release: tag and release link.
446	- Risks and retrospective: what worked, what slowed the team down, next-sprint changes.
447	- Next sprint plan: initial ideas and carryover issues.
448	- New in Sprint 3:
449	  - **Suite health** (keep it short). A baseline table of the test suites relevant to the team (the
450	    packages or areas it works on, not the whole repository): for each suite, the command or CI
451	    workflow and the runner's summary line (passed, failed, skipped) at the Sprint 2 tag
452	    `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` and at the end of the sprint. Use CI results where available; locally, run
453	    only the packages you change. Failures are grouped by cause (e.g. environment-specific, already
454	    broken upstream, flaky, caused by our changes), each cause linking one issue that lists the
455	    affected tests. Any test the team's changes broke is fixed by the end of the sprint;
456	    pre-existing failures only need recording and grouping. Every skipped test and disabled CI
457	    check has a linked issue and a reason in a code comment.
458	  - **Mutation testing:** a link to each member's D6 write-up.
459	  - **Hardening issues:** which issues they are and where they came from.
460	  - **Carryovers:** the Sprint 2 issues carried over, and what changed.
461	- The report covers this sprint's work only. Write the Sprint 3 sections fresh rather than copying
462	  a previous report, and check that tables and links render on GitHub (no escaped `\|` or `\[`).
463
```

1	# AI assistance disclosure — required format
2	
3	Course rule, not an upstream Gitea one. Every contributor discloses their own AI use per issue,
4	**even when no AI was used**. Source: the course AI Log Instructions page and `CONTRIBUTING.md`
5	(AI Contribution Policy). Two separate places, both required. The rest of the PR and issue
6	format is in `COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.
7	
8	## 1. A comment on the issue
9	
10	Posted by each contributor on the **issue** they worked, once their work is done. One comment per
11	person — never edit someone else's. Add later sessions by editing your own table.
12	
13	```markdown
14	### AI Assistance — @your-github-username
15	
16	**Role in this issue:** Implementation
17	
18	| # | Tool | Log | What AI helped with |
19	|---|---|---|---|
20	| 1 | claude-code | [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/blob/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md) | Confirmed the files found during concept location, drafted the template change and tests, ran them |

23	```

28	- **Log** is a full `https://github.com/...` link to the filed log. Relative paths break in issue
29	  comments. File naming is in `ai-logs/README.md`.

31	- **No AI used?** Keep the heading and role line and write `No AI used` in place of the table.

34	
35	Reviewers read the PR, and the review rubric scores "AI transparency", so the PR says how AI was

54	- **Placeholders left in**: `@your-github-username` or the full `Implementation / Code review /

1	---
2	scope: stryker.config.mjs, stryker.vitest.config.ts

5	
6	# mutation testing — StrykerJS for the frontend, go-mutesting for Go
7	
8	**Read when:** running a mutation tool on changed files, writing a personal config, or a run that
9	stops before mutating anything.
10	**Not here:** how each test tier runs -> `testing.md`; the course deliverable and its file names ->
11	`COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.
12	
13	## Responsibilities
14	
15	| Side | Tool | Where it comes from |
16	| --- | --- | --- |
17	| `web_src/js` (Vitest) | StrykerJS with its Vitest runner | `package.json` devDependencies, `stryker.config.mjs` |
18	| Go packages | go-mutesting | `go install`, nothing in `go.mod` |
19	
20	Gremlins is not used: its README warns that very big Go modules can take hours, and Gitea is one
21	module (`go.mod`).
22	
23	## Key files
24	
25	| Path | What it holds |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| `stryker.config.mjs` | Shared Stryker options: the Vitest plugin, ignore patterns read from `.gitignore`, runner, reporters. Names no files |
28	| `stryker.vitest.config.ts` | `vitest.config.ts` merged with `isolate: true`, used only by Stryker |
29	| `vitest.config.ts` | The normal Vitest config, with `isolate: false` |
30	| `.gitignore` | `/.stryker-tmp` (Stryker's sandbox), `/reports/mutation` (its reports), `/report.json` (go-mutesting's) |
31	
32	## Conventions & invariants
33	
34	- `stryker.config.mjs` sets no `mutate`. Personal configs import it, spread it, and change only
35	  report paths or similar; the files to mutate are passed on the command line with `--mutate`.
36	- Stryker copies the project into `.stryker-tmp/` before running. `stryker.config.mjs` feeds every
37	  `.gitignore` line to `ignorePatterns`, which Stryker matches with `.gitignore` semantics (`!`
38	  included), so the copy holds only what git tracks. `node_modules` is symlinked, not copied.
39	- `plugins` names `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` directly. Stryker's default `@stryker-mutator/*`
40	  search looks beside its own package, which pnpm keeps under `node_modules/.pnpm` without the
41	  runner, so the `vitest` option is then reported as unknown.
42	- The Vitest runner's `related` mode (on by default) runs only test files that import the mutated
43	  files, and `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` reruns only the tests covering each mutant.
44	- Stryker runs all related test files in one worker. With `vitest.config.ts`'s `isolate: false`,
45	  module state (such as a listener registered at import) leaks from one file into the next, so
46	  `stryker.vitest.config.ts` turns isolation on. Normal runs and CI keep `vitest.config.ts`.
47	- go-mutesting's built-in test step replaces the real source file with each mutant, runs that
48	  package's tests, and restores it. Only the package's own `_test.go` tests run, not `tests/`.
49	- go-mutesting always writes `report.json` to the directory it runs in; the `json_output` setting
50	  in its YAML config is not read. In its output, `PASS` means the mutant was killed.
51	
52	## Recipes
53	
54	**Run Stryker on some files.** From the repository root:
55	`pnpm exec stryker run <config> --mutate web_src/js/a.ts,web_src/js/b.ts`. The summary table is
56	printed at the end; `mutation.json` and `mutation.html` land in `reports/mutation/` unless the
57	config moves them. A run on one ~250-line module with ~40 related tests takes about a minute.
58	
59	**Write a personal Stryker config.** A `.mjs` file that imports the shared one:
60	
61	```js
62	import base from '<relative path>/stryker.config.mjs';
63	export default {...base, jsonReporter: {fileName: 'reports/mutation/<name>/mutation.json'}};
64	```
65	
66	Paths inside it resolve from the directory Stryker runs in, so run it from the repository root.
67	
68	**Run go-mutesting.**
69	
70	1. Install: `go install github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/cmd/go-mutesting@master`. Its module
71	   path has no `/v2`, so its v2 tags cannot be installed by version, and building it needs the Go
72	   version its own `go.mod` asks for.
73	2. Run on files, with the Go version from `go.mod` so the tests match CI:
74	   `GOTOOLCHAIN=go<version> go-mutesting <file.go>... > <out>.txt`. The last line holds the score.
75	3. Check `git status`: no source file may be left changed. Move `report.json` where it belongs.
76	
77	## Gotchas
78	
79	- Stryker's "There were failed tests in the initial test run" means a related test fails on
80	  unchanged code. Rerun it with `pnpm exec vitest related <file> --run --no-file-parallelism` to see
81	  whether it only fails when files share a worker (an order-dependent test) or fails anyway.
82	- A Stryker `EISDIR ... copyfile` error comes from copying a symlinked directory; any such folder
83	  needs to be in `.gitignore` or `ignorePatterns`.
84	- Mutants that hit Stryker's timeout count as killed, and whether one times out can change between
85	  runs, so two runs of the same code can differ by a mutant or two.
86	- An interrupted go-mutesting run can leave a mutated source file behind. `git diff` shows it;
87	  `git restore <file>` undoes it.
88	- Each go-mutesting mutant recompiles and reruns the whole package's tests, so packages with
89	  database fixtures (`models/...`) are slow: time one `go test ./<pkg>/` first and multiply.
90	- Behaviour covered only by `tests/integration` shows up as surviving go-mutesting mutants.
91	- `make lint-js` lints the root `*.ts` files, not `.mjs` ones, and nothing under `docs/`
92	  (`Makefile`, `ESLINT_FILES`).
93	
94	## Related
95	
96	- `testing.md` — the test tiers the mutation tools run
97	- `build-and-tooling.md` — the lint and build targets
98
```
</details></tool-use>

=== #118
{"assignee":["CarsonRackley"],"body":"Part of #7. Upstream requests: go-gitea/gitea#1415 (badge on the favicon) and go-gitea/gitea#31925 (browser notifications).\n\n### User Story\n\nAs a user who keeps Gitea open in a background tab, I want the tab icon to show when I have unread notifications, and optionally a desktop notification when a new one arrives, so that I notice review requests and mentions without switching back to check.\n\n### User Scenario\n\nMarco keeps Gitea open in one of many browser tabs while he codes. On the Notifications page he clicks \"Enable desktop notifications\", and the browser asks for permission once. He allows it. Later a teammate requests his review. A dot appears on the Gitea tab's icon, and a desktop notification says \"You have 1 new notification\". He clicks it, and the browser switches to Gitea and opens his notifications. After he reads it, the unread count drops to zero and the dot disappears. When he is already looking at Gitea, no desktop notification pops up; the navbar count is enough.\n\n### Acceptance Criteria\n\n- [ ] AC1: Given a signed-in user with at least one unread notification, when any Gitea page loads or the unread count updates, then the tab icon shows a badge dot, and when the count drops to 0 the default icon comes back without a reload.\n- [ ] AC2: Given an Actions run page, which already sets the tab icon to the run's status, when the user also has unread notifications, then the run status icon is shown, not the notification badge.\n- [ ] AC3: Given desktop notifications have never been enabled in this browser, when new notifications arrive, then no desktop notification is shown and the browser never asks for permission on its own.\n- [ ] AC4: Given the user clicks \"Enable desktop notifications\" on the Notifications page, when the browser asks for permission and the user denies it, then the page says notifications are blocked by the browser and the setting stays off.\n- [ ] AC5: Given desktop notifications are enabled and permission is granted, when the unread count goes up while the Gitea tab is hidden, then exactly one desktop notification is shown saying how many new notifications there are, without the issue title or repository name.\n- [ ] AC6: Given Gitea is open in several tabs, when the unread count goes up, then the user gets one desktop notification, not one per tab.\n- [ ] AC7: Given the Gitea tab is visible, or the count stays the same or goes down, when the count updates, then no desktop notification is shown.\n- [ ] AC8: Given a desktop notification is shown, when the user clicks it, then the browser focuses Gitea and opens `/notifications`.\n- [ ] AC9: Given desktop notifications are enabled, when the user clicks \"Disable desktop notifications\", then no more desktop notifications are shown in that browser.\n\n### Out of Scope\n\n- Notifications when no Gitea tab is open (Web Push with a service worker and server-side keys).\n- A number inside the badge, or a count in the page title.\n- Per-type or per-repository rules for which notifications alert.\n- Sounds, email, and the mobile or API side of notifications.\n\n### Open Questions\n\n- Should the badge be something the user can turn off? (Proposed: no. It is passive and only appears when there is something unread.)\n- Should the alert also fire when the page falls back to polling because the event stream is unavailable? (Proposed: yes, both update paths behave the same.)\n\n### Design Decisions\n\n#### Decision 1: The desktop notification opt-in is stored per browser, not on the account\n\n**Decision:** \"Enable desktop notifications\" is remembered in the browser's local storage.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A per-user setting stored on the server, shown in Settings. (b) No stored setting: alert whenever the browser permission is granted.\n**Rationale:** Browser permission is per browser and per device anyway, and browsers only allow the permission prompt after a click. A server-side setting would turn on in a browser that never granted permission and would have to prompt without a click, which browsers block. With (b), users who granted permission for something else could not turn the alerts off without revoking it.\n**Consequences:** No server or schema change. The choice does not follow the user to other browsers, and clearing site data turns it off.\n\n#### Decision 2: The desktop notification shows only a count\n\n**Decision:** The notification text is \"You have N new notifications\" and clicking it opens `/notifications`.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Show the newest notification's issue title and repository. (b) Show one notification per new item, each linking to its issue.\n**Rationale:** The live update only delivers a count, so (a) and (b) need an extra API request per update. Titles from private repositories would also appear on a lock screen or a shared screen. A count is enough to make the user switch tabs.\n**Consequences:** The user cannot tell a review request from a subscription update until they open Gitea. Richer content is follow-up work if users ask for it.\n\n#### Decision 3: Badge as a dot, with Actions run status taking precedence\n\n**Decision:** The badge is a plain dot drawn on the Gitea icon, reusing the drawing code that already badges the icon with an Actions run's status. On a run page the run status wins.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Draw the unread number in the icon. (b) Put the count in the page title, like \"(3) Gitea\".\n**Rationale:** A number is unreadable at 16 px and needs a \"9+\" cap. The title is truncated in a crowded tab bar and changes the text screen readers announce. On a run page the user is watching that run, so its status is the more useful icon.\n**Consequences:** The icon code needs to know which badge currently owns the icon, so leaving a run page or reading every notification restores the right one.\n\n### Scope\n\nmedium\n\n---\nDrafted with Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5).\n","comments":[{"a":"vvchopra","b":"Spec looks good, ACs are testable and the goal is clear. {"assignee":["ab-wm"],"body":"## Summary\nLet a pull request depend on other pull requests and issues, and keep it from merging until they are done, so that dependent changes never land before the code they need.\n\nGitea already does most of this:\n- Adding and removing dependencies on pull requests and issues.\n- Refusing to merge a pull request while one of its dependencies is open, from the merge button, through the API, and for a scheduled merge.\n- Refusing loops of two, and, on the web, self-dependencies.\n- Turning dependencies on or off per repository with \"Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests\".\n\n## User Story\nAs a maintainer reviewing related changes, I want Gitea to block a dependent pull request until its prerequisites merge, so that unfinished dependencies do not break the target branch.\n\n## Sub-issues\n- #143: a pull request that was closed without merging keeps blocking the pull requests that depend on it, and every way of merging refuses with a clear error.\n- #144: the pull request page shows which dependencies block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed. Blocked by #143.\n- #145: loops of any length, and self-dependencies through the API, are refused.\n\nThis issue is closed once all three are.\n\n## Out of Scope\n- A separate setting for merge blocking; the existing \"Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests\" setting decides.\n- Changes to cross-repository dependencies, which Gitea already allows unless the site administrator turns them off.\n- Merging a scheduled pull request the moment its last dependency merges.\n- Automatic rebasing of dependent pull requests, and merge queues.\n\n## Scope\nlarge (8 points), split into #143  (medium, 3 points), #144 (medium, 3 points) and #145 (small, 2 points). CSCI 435/535 — Software Engineering[¶](#csci-435535-software-engineering "Permanent link")
==========================================================================================

Welcome to CSCI 435/535. This semester, six teams will each work on a real, established open-source project using modern agentic AI tooling as part of their software engineering workflow: agile sprints, code review, CI, testing, and real project management.

Announcements[¶](#announcements "Permanent link")
-------------------------------------------------

November 5, 2026 — **New-Tech Showcase 2 is Tuesday, November 10.** Claim your team's tool by **Friday, November 6, at noon** in the Zulip **#showcases** channel. See the [Showcase 2 requirements](showcase2/).

November 4, 2026 — **Sprint 3 is open.** All deliverables are due **November 19 at 11:59 PM**; the mid-sprint check-in (D7), with at least one code PR open or merged, is due **November 12 at 11:59 PM**. New this sprint: **mutation testing** (replaces the UML diagrams), a **Test Evidence** section in every PR, and a **suite health** section in the report. Sprints[¶](#sprints "Permanent link")
=====================================

The project unfolds across **5 sprints (S0–S4)**. Each sprint builds on the previous one: S0 gets everyone set up and working; S1–S3 are the main development sprints; S4 closes the project with a polished release, presentation, and retrospective.

See the [Schedule](../schedule/) for sprint dates and the [Syllabus](../syllabus/#11-project-structure-sprints-presentations-and-showcases) for an overview of the grading structure.

* * *

What every sprint looks like[¶](#what-every-sprint-looks-like "Permanent link")
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Each sprint follows the same basic rhythm:

1.  **Plan** — pull issues from the backlog, assign owners, scope the work.
2.  **Build** — implement features through the full PR workflow (branch → code → test → review → merge).
3.  **Log** — capture all AI interactions as you go (see [AI Log Instructions](../ai-logs/)).
4.  **Report** — write a sprint report summarizing what was done, what was learned, and what comes next.
5.  **Release** — tag a release marking the sprint's end state.
6.  **Reflect** — complete the individual reflection survey.
7.  **Present** — deliver a lightning talk or showcase presentation (schedule varies by sprint).

Detailed requirements for each sprint are on the sprint's own page (links in the table above).

Sprint 3: Project Development & Testing[¶](#sprint-3-project-development-testing "Permanent link")
==================================================================================================

**Nov 3 – Nov 19 · All deliverables due Nov 19, 11:59 PM (mid-sprint check-in due Nov 12) · 100 points (12% of course grade)**

Sprint 3 continues the development of your project and puts the focus on **testing**: how well your tests check what your code is supposed to do. The issue backlog, PR workflow, and general expectations carry forward; see [Sprint 1](../sprint1/) and [Sprint 2](../sprint2/) for anything not explicitly changed here. This page covers what is **new or different** in Sprint 3.

* * *

Sprint 3 at a glance

**Key dates:** Nov 12: check-in + at least one code PR (open or merged) · Nov 19: everything else

**Important rules (they cost the most points):**

*   No merge without an approval on the latest commit.
*   Spec review on the issue, saying what was checked.
*   Every code PR links its issue.
*   Real AI logs.
*   Test Evidence table in every PR; expected values not copied from the code's output.
*   Mutation testing with a tool, before and after reports committed.
*   Your team introduces no new test failures; skipped tests and disabled checks need an issue.

Unfamiliar with a term?

Check the [Glossary](../glossary/) for definitions of terms used throughout this page.

* * *

### Before you begin[¶](#before-you-begin "Permanent link")

*   **Check your AI log setup** against the [AI Log Instructions](../ai-logs/) before your first session.
*   **Read "Things that must improve"** below. These issues were observed in Sprint 2 and will be graded strictly.
*   **Record your baseline early** (see D8): the test results at your Sprint 2 release tag (`-csci435-s2`), from CI or by running the relevant test suites locally. It helps you find hardening issues and get the mutation tool running.
*   **Try the mutation testing tool early** (see D6), on any existing file in the part of the code you work on. Do not wait until your PRs are ready.

* * *

### What is new in Sprint 3[¶](#what-is-new-in-sprint-3 "Permanent link")

*   **Mutation testing** (D6): a new individual deliverable. It **replaces** the UML diagrams from Sprint 2.
*   **Test evidence section** in every PR description (D4).
*   **Hardening issues**: one of your issues may be a hardening issue (D1).
*   **Suite health section** in the sprint report (D8).
*   **Mid-sprint check-in requires an open PR** (D7), due Nov 12.

Team feature for Sprints 3–4

Each team will be assigned a larger feature that spans Sprints 3 and 4. The instructor or TA will post it as an issue in your team's issue tracker and notify your team when it is posted. You will likely need to split it into sub-issues.

* * *

### Things that must improve from Sprint 2[¶](#things-that-must-improve-from-sprint-2 "Permanent link")

These issues were observed in Sprint 2 and will be graded strictly in Sprint 3.

**1\. Open PRs early.** In Sprint 2, most PRs were opened in the last two days, which left no time for review. In Sprint 3, you need a code PR by the mid-sprint check-in (see D7).

**2\. Independent approval before merging.** A PR is merged only after a teammate approves its **latest commit**. Merging without an approval, or after pushing new commits since the approval, is not allowed. Once approved, the author may merge. To keep reviews moving, request the review on GitHub and notify your reviewer on Zulip; reviewers respond (approve or request changes) within 24 hours.

**3\. Spec reviews must be visible and show what was checked.** Before coding starts, a teammate posts a review comment on the issue itself. The comment states what the reviewer checked: whether each acceptance criterion is clear and testable, which cases were considered (and whether they are covered), and whether the scope fits. If the reviewer finds problems, they list them and the author updates the spec. If the spec is good, the reviewer says so and approves, but "Looks good!" with nothing about what was checked is not acceptable.

**4\. Link PRs and issues.** Every code PR must link the issue it addresses, so the PR can be checked against the spec. Use `Closes #<issue>` in the PR description so the issue closes automatically when the PR is merged, and attach issues and code PRs to the `Sprint 3` milestone.

**5\. AI logs must be real logs.** A log shows your prompts and the AI's output (SpecStory format recommended; see the [AI Log Instructions](../ai-logs/)). The following are **not** logs and receive no full credit: summaries of a session, paraphrased prompts, a share link to a chat, or tool output without the prompts that produced it. File names must follow `YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`. Link the log from the issue or PR it documents.

**6\. The sprint report must render.** Check that tables and links display correctly on GitHub (no escaped `\|` or `\[`). Use the Sprint 3 sections, not a copy of a previous report.

* * *

### Deliverables[¶](#deliverables "Permanent link")

#### D1 - Sprint Backlog[¶](#d1-sprint-backlog "Permanent link")

Same process as Sprint 2 ([D1](../sprint2/#d1-sprint-backlog)), including the priority on carryovers: unfinished Sprint 2 issues go into your Sprint 3 backlog first, or you document on the issue why they are dropped.

**Scope minimums for Sprint 3** (same as Sprint 2):

Role

Minimum issues

Each CSCI 435 member

at least 2 medium issues (or equivalent story points)

Each CSCI 535 (grad) member

at least 2 medium issues + 1 additional small issue (or equivalent story points)

**Scope must be justified.** Each issue states its scope (small or medium) and one or two sentences on why: which components it touches and how much change you expect. The instructor or TA may reclassify an issue whose scope is clearly overstated.

**Hardening issues (optional).** One of your issues may be a _hardening issue_: work that makes the existing system more reliable rather than adding a feature. Good sources:

*   **Your baseline run** (see D8): failing tests, flaky tests, or broken CI checks on `main`.
*   **Tech debt your team recorded** in the "Introduced" and "Encountered" fields of your Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 PRs.
*   **Known bugs** found in reviews, after merging, or by teammates.
*   **The upstream issue tracker**, for bugs in the parts of the system your team works on.

A hardening issue is scoped like any other issue (see the scope justification above). It must also include evidence that the problem is fixed:

*   **Bug fix:** a test that fails before the fix and passes after.
*   **Flaky test:** the root cause, and enough repeated runs of that test before and after the fix to show the change (for example, 20 runs for a unit test or 10 for an E2E test).
*   **Broken or missing CI check:** links to CI runs before and after the fix.
*   **Failing tests in the baseline:** pass/fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group of failures.

Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause counts as small at most.

**Team feature.** When the team feature issue is posted (see the box under "What is new in Sprint 3"), split it into sub-issues, each with its own owner, spec (D2), and scope. Link each sub-issue to the feature issue. Sub-issues count toward your scope minimum like any other issue. When the feature is posted, add its sub-issues to your Sprint 3 milestone and adjust your backlog as needed.

Create a `Sprint 3` milestone in GitHub and attach all selected issues to it.

**What to provide in D8 (Sprint report):** link to the Sprint 3 milestone and the rationale for your backlog decisions.

* * *

#### D2 - Requirements Specification[¶](#d2-requirements-specification "Permanent link")

Same format and requirements as Sprint 1 ([D2](../sprint1/#d2-requirements-specification)). Specs must be written and reviewed before coding begins; see item 3 in "Things that must improve" for what counts as a review.

Hardening issues use a bug format (include the observed and expected behaviors, the steps to reproduct the issue, and other details about the issue) when they fix a defect. Otherwise, use a short task format: the problem, the goal, acceptance criteria, and other necessary details.

* * *

#### D3 - Design Decisions[¶](#d3-design-decisions "Permanent link")

Same as Sprint 2 ([D3](../sprint2/#d3-design-decisions)): each decision names at least two concrete alternatives and explains the choice.

* * *

#### D4 - Code Changes and Pull Requests[¶](#d4-code-changes-and-pull-requests "Permanent link")

Same workflow as Sprint 2 ([D4](../sprint2/#d4-code-changes-and-pull-requests)), including **the Tech Debt section**. Sprint 3 adds a **Test Evidence** section to every PR description. It replaces the "how it was tested" part of the description, so you don't write it twice.

`## Test Evidence  | Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value | |---|---|---|---| | AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |  **Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]  **AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]`

How to fill it in:

*   **One row per acceptance criterion** from D2. For bug reports, use the Expected Behavior instead. For PRs that change no product behavior (for example, CI changes), write "N/A" and explain why.
*   **Test(s):** the test name (and file, if not obvious). If you checked the AC manually, write `Manual:` followed by the steps and what you saw. If an AC is tested both automatically and manually, list both in the same row.
*   **Level:** `unit`, `integration`, `E2E`, or `manual`.
*   **Source of expected value:** where the expected result in your test comes from. Use one of: `AC`, `issue discussion`, `docs`, `upstream behavior`, or `other` (explain). **The current output of your own code is not a valid source**; a test whose expected value was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
*   **Not tested automatically, and why:** only for ACs checked manually only.
*   You may use AI to draft this section, but you are responsible for checking that it is accurate.

Example:

Acceptance criterion

Test(s)

Level

Source of expected value

AC1: An end date before the start date is rejected with an error

`outOfOffice.schema.test.ts` > rejects end before start

unit

AC

AC2: The away badge appears on the booking page during the out-of-office window

`booking-ooo.e2e.ts` > shows away badge in window

E2E

AC

AC3: The badge text is readable in dark mode

Manual: enabled dark mode, opened the booking page during the window → badge text is readable

manual

issue discussion

**Not tested automatically, and why:** AC3 depends on visual contrast, which our test setup does not check.

**If your fork has no CI** that runs your tests, include in the PR description the command(s) you ran and a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).

**Reviewers** add one line to the code review rubric ([Sprint 1, D4](../sprint1/#d4-code-changes-and-pull-requests)):

Criterion

Score (1–10)

Notes

Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally?

* * *

#### D5 - AI Logs[¶](#d5-ai-logs "Permanent link")

Same requirements as Sprint 1 ([D5](../sprint1/#d5-ai-logs)) and the [AI Log Instructions](../ai-logs/), with the enforcement described in item 5 of "Things that must improve."

**Log storage:** `ai-logs/sprint3/<your-github-username>/`

* * *

#### D6 - Mutation Testing _(new)_[¶](#d6-mutation-testing-new "Permanent link")

This is a new individual deliverable.

**What it is.** A mutation testing tool makes small changes to your code (_mutants_), such as flipping a condition or changing a boundary value, and runs your tests against each one. If a test fails, the mutant is _killed_. If all tests pass, the mutant _survived_: your tests did not notice that the code changed. Survivors point to weak or missing tests.

**What to do.** For **one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests** (CSCI 535: **two** such issues; your small issue may be one of them):

1.  Run a mutation testing tool on the **source files changed by your PR(s)** for that issue. Do not run it on the whole project.
2.  Using the tool's report, analyze every surviving mutant: is it _equivalent_ (it behaves exactly like the original code, so no test can kill it), or does it reveal a gap in your tests? If there are more than 10 surviving mutants, analyze at least 10, starting with those in lines your PR added or changed.
3.  Add or strengthen **at least one test that kills a surviving mutant** that revealed a gap. Re-run the tool to confirm it is killed. If no surviving mutant reveals a gap (all are killed or equivalent), say so and justify it in the surviving-mutants table; that completes this step.
4.  **Answer the questions in the template below**.

**Evidence.** Configure the tool to write a machine-readable report (StrykerJS: add `"json"` to `reporters`; Gremlins: `--output=<file>.json`; go-mutesting: save the terminal output to a text file). Commit the report from your first run and from your re-run as `docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json` and `-after.json` (`.txt` for go-mutesting). The mutation scores you list must match the reports, and the mutant your new test kills must show as killed in the "after" report.

**A tool is required.** Manual mutation does not count.

Stack

Tool

TypeScript/JavaScript with Vitest (Actual Budget, Cal.diy, Excalidraw, Outline, Gitea frontend)

[StrykerJS](https://stryker-mutator.io/) with the [Vitest runner](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/vitest-runner/)

TypeScript/JavaScript with Jest (Medusa)

[StrykerJS](https://stryker-mutator.io/) with the [Jest runner](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/jest-runner/)

Go (Gitea backend)

[Gremlins](https://gremlins.dev/) or [go-mutesting](https://github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting)

**Set it up early.** Getting the tool to work on a large codebase is real work: builds, services, and choosing which tests run. Each student configures and runs the tool for their own files and commits the configuration they used. You may reuse a teammate's setup (and are encouraged to), as long as you run the tool yourself and credit the teammate in your report.

**Common problems** to watch for:

*   **The tool stops before mutating.** Tools first run your tests on the unchanged code. If any of the selected tests fail, the run stops. Fix or exclude failing tests first (this is where your baseline run helps).
*   **Tests run against built code.** If your tests run against compiled output (for example, a `dist` folder) instead of the source, mutants in the source are never seen by the tests. Configure the tool to rebuild before testing, or choose tests that run on source.
*   **Tests need services.** Some test suites need a database or another service running. Start them before running the tool.
*   **False survivors.** If you limit which tests run (for example, with Vitest's `dir` option), make sure the tests that cover the mutated files are included. Otherwise, mutants that some test would catch are reported as survived or not covered. Before writing a new test for a survivor, check that the relevant tests actually ran.
*   **Long runs.** Mutating only the files changed by your PR keeps run time manageable.

If you are blocked

If you cannot get the tool to run, first ask your teammates: someone may already have a working setup. If you are still stuck, tell the TA **as early as possible**, with the errors you got and the AI log of what you tried. The TA will help you debug it. If it still cannot be made to work, the TA may approve running the tool on a different issue or a different part of your code instead. Problems reported at the end of the sprint will not excuse a missing D6.

**Submission:** `docs/sprint3/mutation/<issue#>-<username>.md`, using this template:

``# Mutation testing: Issue #<N> -- <issue title>  **PR(s):** #...  **Tool:** ...  **Config:** [link; credit the teammate if you reused their setup]  **Command:** `...` **Reports:** [before](reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json) · [after](reports/<issue#>-<username>-after.json) **Mutation score:** before ...% → after ...%  ## Surviving mutants  | Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why | |---|---|---|---| | | | | |  ## New or strengthened test  Commit: [link] · Test: [file > test name] · Kills: [mutant location]  ## Questions  1. What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests? 2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements? Explain. 3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct? If AI was not used, write "N/A."``

#### D7 - Mid-Sprint Check-in[¶](#d7-mid-sprint-check-in "Permanent link")

**Due: Nov 12, 11:59 PM.**

**Submission:** `docs/sprint3/checkin/<username>.md`

**Format:** ~100 words per question, plus a link.

1.  What have you implemented so far, and what remains?
2.  What is one thing you learned about testing in your project?
3.  What is one risk to finishing your work by Nov 19, and what will you do about it?

**Required link:** at least one **code PR you authored**, open and ready for review, or merged, by Nov 12.

#### D8 - Sprint Report[¶](#d8-sprint-report "Permanent link")

Same format as Sprint 1 ([D6 in Sprint 1](../sprint1/#d6-sprint-report)), with these additions:

*   **Suite health** (new section). Keep it short:
    *   **Baseline table** for the test suites relevant to your team (the packages or areas you work on, not the whole repository). For each suite: the command or CI workflow, and the test runner's summary line (passed, failed, skipped) at your **Sprint 2 release tag** (`-csci435-s2`) and at the **end** of the sprint. Use CI results where available; if you run tests locally, run only the packages you change.
    *   **Failures grouped by cause** (for example: environment-specific, already broken upstream, flaky, caused by our changes), with a link to one issue per cause that lists the affected tests.
    *   **No failures introduced by your team.** Any test your team's changes broke must be fixed by the end of the sprint. Pre-existing failures only need to be recorded and grouped; fixing them is optional (and can be a hardening issue).
    *   **Skipped tests and disabled CI checks.** Skipping a test or disabling a CI check requires a linked issue and a reason in a code comment.
*   **Mutation testing:** links to each member's D6 file.
*   **Hardening issues:** which issues they are and where they came from.
*   Carryovers from Sprint 2 and what changed.

**Submit to:** `docs/sprint3/report.md` (or `.pdf`, `.docx`). If you submit Markdown, check that it renders on GitHub.

16	const badgeY = faviconViewBoxHeight - badgeDrawSize - badgeMargin;
17	const badgeScale = badgeDrawSize / badgeIconSize;
18	// white ring behind the badge so it stands out from the logo, like GitHub's favicon
19	const badgeCenter = badgeDrawSize / 2;
20	const badgeRingRadius = badgeCenter + badgeDrawSize * 0.08;
21	
22	let currentStatus: ActionsStatus | null = null;
23	const defaultFaviconHrefs = new Map<HTMLLinkElement, string>();
24	const faviconDataUrlCache = new Map<ActionsStatus, string>();

30	    defaultFaviconHrefs.set(link, link.href);

34	function resolveTailwindTextColor(colorClass: string): string {
35	  if (!colorProbe) {
36	    colorProbe = document.createElement('span');
37	    colorProbe.style.display = 'none';
38	    document.body.append(colorProbe);
39	  }
40	  colorProbe.className = colorClass;
41	  return getComputedStyle(colorProbe).color || '#000000';
42	}

44	function buildStatusIconMarkup(status: ActionsStatus): string {
45	  const {name, colorClass} = getActionStatusIcon(status, 'circle-fill');
46	  const color = resolveTailwindTextColor(colorClass);
47	  const {svgInnerHtml} = svgParseOuterInner(name);
48	  const coloredInner = svgInnerHtml.replaceAll('currentColor', color);
49	  const ring = html`<circle cx="${badgeX + badgeCenter}" cy="${badgeY + badgeCenter}" r="${badgeRingRadius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`;
50	  const badge = html`<g data-actions-status-name="${status}" transform="translate(${badgeX}, ${badgeY}) scale(${badgeScale})" fill="${color}" color="${color}">${htmlRaw(coloredInner)}</g>`;
51	  return html`${htmlRaw(ring)}${htmlRaw(badge)}`;
52	}

62	  faviconDataUrlCache.set(status, dataUrl);

=== #143 scope format
## Out of Scope
- Showing on the pull request page which dependencies block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed: Issue (#144)
- Dependency loops of three or more, and the checks the API skips when a dependency is added: Issue (#145)
- Merging a scheduled pull request the moment its last dependency merges. As today, it is tried again when its checks or reviews next change.
- Letting administrators merge past a dependency. "Merge anyway" does not skip dependencies today, and that stays.
- "Mark as manually merged", which records a merge made outside Gitea and does not check dependencies, as today.
- A separate setting for merge blocking. The existing "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" setting decides (AC7).
- Adding and removing dependencies, which Gitea already supports.
- Merge queues, and rebasing dependent pull requests automatically.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
medium (3 points). Touches the rule that decides whether a dependency is resolved, and the three ways a pull request gets merged (the merge button, the API and a scheduled merge) with their error messages; a small change in each, plus tests for every path.

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing.

Spec reviewed — @controlled-opposition

**Acceptance criteria:** AC1–AC7 are each clear and testable; each names a merge path, a dependency state and an observable result (message, status code, or merged or not).
**Cases considered:** Web, API and auto-merge; every dependency kind and state in the table; closing a blocked PR; dependencies turned off; admin and manual merge (out of scope). All covered.
**Scope:** Medium fits: one rule change plus three merge paths.
**Verdict:** Approved.

class Source {
  url: string;
  eventSource: EventSource | null;
  listening: Record<string, boolean>;
  clients: Array<MessagePort>;

  constructor(url: string) {
    this.url = url;
    this.eventSource = new EventSource(url);
    this.listening = {};
    this.clients = [];
    this.listen('open');
    this.listen('close');
    this.listen('logout');
    this.listen('notification-count');
    this.listen('stopwatches');
    this.listen('error');
  }

  register(port: MessagePort) {
    if (this.clients.includes(port)) return;

    this.clients.push(port);

    port.postMessage({
      type: 'status',
      message: `registered to ${this.url}`,
    });
  }

  deregister(port: MessagePort) {
    const portIdx = this.clients.indexOf(port);
    if (portIdx < 0) {
      return this.clients.length;
    }
    this.clients.splice(portIdx, 1);
    return this.clients.length;
  }

9	Marco keeps Gitea open in one of many browser tabs while he codes. On the Notifications page he clicks "Enable desktop notifications", and the browser asks for permission once. He allows it. Later a teammate requests his review. A dot appears on the Gitea tab's icon, and a desktop notification says "You have 1 new notification". He clicks it, and the browser switches to Gitea and opens his notifications. After he reads it, the unread count drops to zero and the dot disappears. When he is already looking at Gitea, no desktop notification pops up; the navbar count is enough.
10	
11	### Acceptance Criteria
12	
13	- [ ] AC1: Given a signed-in user with at least one unread notification, when any Gitea page loads or the unread count updates, then the tab icon shows a badge dot, and when the count drops to 0 the default icon comes back without a reload.
14	- [ ] AC2: Given an Actions run page, which already sets the tab icon to the run's status, when the user also has unread notifications, then the run status icon is shown, not the notification badge.
15	- [ ] AC3: Given desktop notifications have never been enabled in this browser, when new notifications arrive, then no desktop notification is shown and the browser never asks for permission on its own.
16	- [ ] AC4: Given the user clicks "Enable desktop notifications" on the Notifications page, when the browser asks for permission and the user denies it, then the page says notifications are blocked by the browser and the setting stays off.
17	- [ ] AC5: Given desktop notifications are enabled and permission is granted, when the unread count goes up while the Gitea tab is hidden, then exactly one desktop notification is shown saying how many new notifications there are, without the issue title or repository name.
18	- [ ] AC6: Given Gitea is open in several tabs, when the unread count goes up, then the user gets one desktop notification, not one per tab.
19	- [ ] AC7: Given the Gitea tab is visible, or the count stays the same or goes down, when the count updates, then no desktop notification is shown.
20	- [ ] AC8: Given a desktop notification is shown, when the user clicks it, then the browser focuses Gitea and opens `/notifications`.
21	- [ ] AC9: Given desktop notifications are enabled, when the user clicks "Disable desktop notifications", then no more desktop notifications are shown in that browser.
22	
23	### Out of Scope
24	
25	- Notifications when no Gitea tab is open (Web Push with a service worker and server-side keys).
26	- A number inside the badge, or a count in the page title.
27	- Per-type or per-repository rules for which notifications alert.
28	- Sounds, email, and the mobile or API side of notifications.
29	
30	### Open Questions
31	
32	- Should the badge be something the user can turn off? (Proposed: no. It is passive and only appears when there is something unread.)
33	- Should the alert also fire when the page falls back to polling because the event stream is unavailable? (Proposed: yes, both update paths behave the same.)
34	
35	### Design Decisions
36	
37	#### Decision 1: The desktop notification opt-in is stored per browser, not on the account

I've drafted the #118 spec changes and posted nothing. The two `.gitkeep` files are restored, so `main` is clean.

You asked for the milestone and scope fixes, but I also went further: checking the spec against the code turned up gaps a strict reviewer could flag.

## Proposed changes

| Section | Change | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Adds "3 points" and lists the files it touches; frontend only | D1 requires a justification. The 3 points match how #143 sizes medium |
| **AC2** | The badge comes back when a run's status icon is cleared without a reload | `RepoActionView.vue` resets the icon itself, and only Decision 3 mentioned this case |
| **AC4** | Also covers permission that was already blocked | The browser won't prompt in that case, so "denies it" didn't cover it |
| **AC5, AC7** | "Every tab hidden" and "any tab visible" replace "the Gitea tab" | With two tabs open, a hidden one could alert while you're looking at the other, which your user scenario rules out |
| **AC5** | N is the rise in the count, not total unread; both update paths count | Your tests need a stated expected value, and this also settles your polling question |
| **AC10 (new)** | No desktop notification on page load or reload | A background tab reloading with unread items has no earlier count to compare against |
| **AC11 (new)** | A failed poll doesn't cause a false alert | `updateNotificationCount` returns 0 on error (`notification.ts:123-125`), so a simple comparison would see 0 → N as a rise |
| **AC12 (new)** | Browsers without notification support get a message, and the badge still works | The spec didn't cover this case |
| **Open Questions** | Both marked resolved, using your proposed answers | These are your calls, so change them if you've changed your mind |
| **Decision 4 (new)** | How tabs avoid duplicate or unwanted alerts | This is the hardest design choice in the issue, and the spec didn't cover it |

## Decide before posting
1. **Do you want Decision 4 and the stricter AC5/AC7?** I recommend yes, since an alert while you're looking at Gitea is what the story says shouldn't happen, but it's the biggest addition.
    - **How it works:** a hidden tab asks the others over `BroadcastChannel` whether any is visible, and a fixed notification `tag` collapses duplicates.
    - **Risk:** nothing in `web_src/js` uses `BroadcastChannel` yet, and I haven't tried this in a browser.
    - **Simpler alternative:** use `tag` alone and list the visible-tab case under Out of Scope, which helps with the Nov 12 deadline.
2. **Is that meaning of "visible" OK?** It follows the browser's Page Visibility state. If Gitea is the active tab in a window behind your editor, it counts as visible and won't alert, which could be a surprise for the "Marco" scenario.

## Rule checks
- **You opened #118:** my notes from Sprint 0 say you should implement issues someone else opened. The Sprint 3 page doesn't repeat that rule and ab-wm also owns issues, but check that it no longer applies.
- **Defending the spec:** I found these gaps by reading the code myself. Sprint 0 expects you to find the relevant code yourself before using AI, so read `notification.ts` and `favicon-status.ts` first, because you'll need to explain each change.
- **Spec review:** the edits make vvchopra's approval out of date, so post them first and then ask a teammate for a review that names what was checked. I'd also leave that wording to them.

## Things to watch when you implement it
- **Button:** `notification.ts:96` replaces all of `#notification_div` on every count update, so the enable button gets replaced too and needs setting up again.
- **Default icon:** `rememberDefaultFaviconHrefs` saves whatever icon is set the first time it runs, so if the badge is applied first, it could be saved as the "default".

Closes #143

## What changed and why

A pull request that depends on another pull request could be merged as soon as that one was closed, even if it was never merged, so unfinished work could reach the target branch. This PR keeps it blocked until the pull requests it depends on are actually merged. Dependencies on issues work as before: closing the issue is enough.

- **Merging has its own dependency rule.** For merging, a dependency now counts as done only when it is a closed issue or a merged pull request. Closing keeps the old rule, where closed is enough, so a pull request whose dependency was closed without merging can still be closed.

- **The merge button says why.** Pressing Merge shows "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." This is a new message: the old one, still shown when closing is blocked, only asks for issues to be closed.
- **The API refuses with 405 instead of 500.** It gives the same sentence, like its other reasons for refusing a merge. Before, an open dependency made it answer 500 Internal Server Error.
- **Turning dependencies off stops them from blocking merges.** With "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" off, dependencies are hidden and can't be removed, yet they still blocked the merge. The merge now ignores them, as closing already did.

2	=== BODY
3	Closes #143
4	
5	## What changed and why
6	
7	A pull request that depends on another pull request could be merged as soon as that one was closed, even if it was never merged, so unfinished work could reach the target branch. This PR keeps it blocked until the pull requests it depends on are actually merged. Dependencies on issues work as before: closing the issue is enough.
8	
9	- **Merging has its own dependency rule.** For merging, a dependency now counts as done only when it is a closed issue or a merged pull request. Closing keeps the old rule, where closed is enough, so a pull request whose dependency was closed without merging can still be closed.
10	- **All three ways of merging follow it.** The merge button, the API and a scheduled "merge when checks succeed" all pass through the same check before merging, so one change covers all three.
11	- **The merge button says why.** Pressing Merge shows "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." This is a new message: the old one, still shown when closing is blocked, only asks for issues to be closed.
12	- **The API refuses with 405 instead of 500.** It gives the same sentence, like its other reasons for refusing a merge. Before, an open dependency made it answer 500 Internal Server Error.
13	- **Turning dependencies off stops them from blocking merges.** With "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" off, dependencies are hidden and can't be removed, yet they still blocked the merge. The merge now ignores them, as closing already did.
14	- The docs in `.claude-students` describe how merging and closing check dependencies differently, and that fixture repositories have dependencies turned off.
15	
16	## :warning: BREAKING :warning:
17	
18	A pull request that was closed without being merged never put its work in the target branch, so the pull requests that depend on it must not be merged either; that is why merges that used to go through are now refused.
19	
20	- **Some merges that used to go through are now refused.** While dependencies are turned on, a pull request that depends on a pull request closed without merging can no longer be merged, from the merge button, the API or a scheduled merge. To merge it, reopen and merge the pull request it depends on, or remove that dependency from the sidebar.
21	- **The merge API answers 405 instead of 500.** When dependencies block a merge, `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/merge` now answers 405 Method Not Allowed with "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." instead of 500 Internal Server Error. Scripts should treat it like the endpoint's other 405 refusals: resolve the dependencies, then try again.
22	- **With dependencies turned off, they no longer block merging.** A pull request in such a repository used to be refused (the API answered 500) because of dependencies that were hidden and could not be removed; it now merges, as closing already ignored them.
23	
24	## How the changes relate to the ACs
25	
26	- **AC1:** Pressing Merge on B while A is closed without being merged shows the new message, and B is not merged.
27	- **AC2:** The API answers 405 Method Not Allowed with the same sentence, and B is not merged.
28	- **AC3:** A scheduled merge runs the same check when B's checks succeed, so B is not merged, stays open, and stays scheduled to be tried again on its next change.
29	- **AC4:** Once A is merged, B merges from the web and through the API as before.
30	- **AC5:** A dependency on an issue blocks while the issue is open and stops blocking once it is closed, as before.
31	- **AC6:** Closing B uses the closing rule, which treats A as done, so B closes as before.
32	- **AC7:** With dependencies turned off, the merge check skips them, so B merges.
33
